Reading the site"},{"line":10,"text":""},{"line":11,"text":"The plot is not a flat platform with a building on it; the 18 m cross-fall is the dominant design fact. At 100 m up-slope with 18 m of rise, the average grade is ~18%, which is beyond comfortable pedestrian route gradients (typically 1:20 / 5% preferred, 1:12 / 8.3% absolute maximum for ramps) and well beyond accessible route limits over any distance. That single number drives the whole concept: **the building must absorb the level change internally rather than the site being flattened to suit it.**"},{"line":12,"text":""},{"line":13,"text":"Key consequences:"},{"line":14,"text":""},{"line":15,"text":"- **Cut-and-fill balance is the first economic question.** A single-level platform would require either ~18 m of cut at the uphill edge or ~18 m of fill at the downhill edge \u2014 both are large earthworks, and deep fill on a slope is a settlement and stability liability. I will not pursue a single platform."},{"line":16,"text":"- **Terracing is the organising move.** Two or three terraces, each tied to a building level, keeps cut and fill local and modest, and lets each terrace drain to its own edge."},{"line":17,"text":"- **Retaining is unavoidable** at every terrace edge and along the uphill cut face. These are structural elements, not landscape trim, and they need geotechnical design (see \u00a72)."},{"line":18,"text":"- **Drainage is a slope problem, not a roof problem.** Surface water arriving from up-slope must be intercepted *above* the building and carried around it in a cut-off drain; water falling on terraces must be collected and discharged to a controlled outfall, not allowed to sheet down the slope face. Uncontrolled down-slope discharge is the classic trigger for slope instability and for undermining retaining wall foundations."},{"line":19,"text":"- **Access gradient.** Vehicle access (service, deliveries, ambulance/fire) needs a route at or below ~1:8 (12.5%) with a short 1:6 (16.7%) maximum only if unavoidable, and it must be a *route*, not a ramp \u2014 so the access road should run diagonally across the slope (traversing) rather than straight up it. Pedestrian accessible routes should be near-level within each terrace, with the level change taken by lifts and by short, generously-landing ramps or stepped routes with a parallel accessible alternative."},{"line":20,"text":""},{"line":21,"text":"## 2. Geotechnical approach"},{"line":22,"text":""},{"line":23,"text":"Given the slope, the geotechnical scope is materially larger than a flat-site survey:"},{"line":24,"text":""},{"line":25,"text":"1. **Ground investigation before any layout is fixed.** Boreholes/test pits on a grid across the whole footprint *and* across the terrace edges and retaining lines \u2014 not one central hole. I need the depth to a competent bearing stratum, the presence and dip of any weaker layer, groundwater level and its seasonal variation, and the shear strength parameters for slope stability analysis."},{"line":26,"text":"2. **Slope stability analysis** for both the existing slope and the post-construction slope, including the temporary condition during excavation (a cut face is at its most vulnerable before the building and drainage are in). Where walls are tall or the retained slope is significant, consider soil-nailed or anchored solutions rather than a simple cantilever."},{"line":28,"text":"4. **Foundations.** I expect to step footings down the slope, keeping column bases on consistent strata and founding below the frost/seasonal-movement zone. There is no natural fall to shed surface water, so the first design move is not architectural but hydrological."},{"line":13,"text":""},{"line":14,"text":"**Approach:**"},{"line":15,"text":""},{"line":16,"text":"- **Set a finished floor level (FFL) above surrounding ground** \u2014 a raised plinth of 450\u2013600 mm over the external ground level, with a graded apron falling away from the building on all sides. Zoning and footprint concept"},{"line":25,"text":""},{"line":26,"text":"Working assumption: a mid-sized law faculty of roughly **1,800\u20132,200 m\u00b2 gross floor area**, delivered as a **2\u20133 storey building** rather than a sprawling single storey. On a 60 \u00d7 60 m plot this leaves genuine external space \u2014 a forecourt, a courtyard, and service access \u2014 instead of paving the whole site."},{"line":27,"text":""},{"line":28,"text":"**Zoning, in plan:**"},{"line":29,"text":""},{"line":30,"text":"| Zone | Location | Rationale |"},{"line":31,"text":"|---|---|---|"},{"line":32,"text":"| Entrance forecourt / plaza | Street-facing edge | Arrival, identity, and the public face of the faculty; also the main hardstanding that must be graded to drain |"},{"line":33,"text":"| Cafeteria / canteen pavilion | Street-facing corner, at ground level, with its own external door | It serves the whole campus, not just law students \u2014 it should be reachable without entering the teaching block, and it should be able to operate outside faculty hours |"},{"line":34,"text":"| Teaching block (lecture halls, classrooms, seminar rooms) | Central / rear, stacked over 2\u20133 floors | The acoustic and structural core of the building; large column-free halls want to sit over each other with a common structural grid |"},{"line":35,"text":"| Staff offices | Quiet side, upper floors, away from the cafeteria and from the main circulation | Needs daylight, acoustic separation from teaching and from kitchen noise/smell |"},{"line":36,"text":"| Service yard (kitchen deliveries, refuse, plant) | Rear, screened, separate vehicle route | Kitchen deliveries and waste must not cross the student entrance; grease and refuse handling needs its own hardstanding and drainage |"},{"line":37,"text":""},{"line":38,"text":"**Key planning moves:**"},{"line":39,"text":""},{"line":40,"text":"- **Separate the pedestrian and service routes completely.** The kitchen's delivery door and the refuse store go at the rear; the cafeteria's customer entrance faces the plaza. This plan finalises the footprint/zoning and the material choices for the Faculty of

## 1. Site and foundation strategy (finalised)

The site is flat and level, so the governing design problems are **water** and
**differential ground behaviour**, not cut-and-fill or slope stability.

**Levels and drainage.**
- Finished floor level (FFL) set **450–600 mm above surrounding external ground** on a
  raised plinth, with a graded perimeter apron falling away from the building on all
  sides (minimum 1:60). *(Raised from the 300–450 mm in my own survey — see §6.)*
- Positive, designed drainage: perimeter ring drainage with a gravity connection to the
  site outfall. Because the site is flat, the **outfall invert depth governs** how much
  of the site drains by gravity; if it is shallow, a short pumped or attenuation-based
  solution is required for the cafeteria wet areas. Confirm by drainage survey before the
  footprint is frozen.
- Attenuation (below-ground crate storage or a shallow basin) is likely to be required,
  since a flat site cannot shed water quickly.

**Ground investigation (finalised scope).**
- A **borehole / trial-pit grid across the whole footprint** — not one central hole —
  plus a pit at the cafeteria corner, to establish stratum continuity, depth and
  thickness of each layer, the bearing stratum actually selected, its allowable bearing
  pressure, and whether any layer is shrinkable clay, loose fill or organic.
- **Check for a perched water table** sitting on a lower-permeability stratum. This
  matters more than the regional water table: it drives foundation depth, drainage design
  and whether any below-ground accommodation is viable. *(Added from the Medicine survey
  — see §6.)*
- **No basement.** On a flat, layered site with a possible perched water table, a
  basement buys little (the plot is large enough to build at grade) and adds
  waterproofing, dewatering and settlement risk.

**Foundations (finalised).**
- Standard shallow **reinforced-concrete pad footings** under columns and **strip
  footings** under load-bearing walls, founded on the verified bearing stratum at a
  consistent depth.
- **Keep column bases on the same stratum**; where a layer boundary crosses the
  footprint, **step or locally deepen** footings across it rather than letting part of the
  building bear on a different layer.
- A **reinforced ground-beam / tie-beam grid** stitching the pad footings together is a
  firm part of the design (not an option): it is the cheapest way to redistribute
  settlement across a stratum transition and it stiffens the building against the
  layered-soil risk.
- A **stiffened strip or raft** is held in reserve for any bay that cannot avoid a
  stratum transition — in particular under the large-span lecture halls and under the
  cafeteria, which are the most heavily loaded and most service-dense areas.
- **Movement tolerance:** ground-floor slabs and drainage runs detailed to tolerate small
  differential movement — movement joints, flexible service connections, and slab
  reinforcement detailed for it.
- No piling is anticipated on the given information; hold piling in reserve only if the
  boreholes reveal a soft layer thicker than ~2 m beneath the cafeteria or a high perched
  water table.

## 2. Footprint and zoning (finalised)

**Concept: a single compact 2-storey main block with a clearly separated, single-storey
cafeteria wing.**

- **Footprint:** main block roughly **45 m × 30 m (~1,350 m² per floor)** plus a
  cafeteria wing of roughly **25 m × 18 m (~450 m²)**, leaving generous circulation, a
  forecourt and service access within the 60 m × 60 m plot. Total built area in the order

  consume most of the plot and leave no room for the service yard and drainage, so two

**Circulation.** A single central spine with two stairs and a lift; the cafeteria wing

bays where a clear span is needed. Repetitive foundations are exactly what the layered-soil
condition rewards.

- **Movement tolerance:** ground-floor slabs and drainage runs detailed to tolerate small
  differential movement — movement joints, flexible service connections, and slab
  reinforcement detailed for it.
- No piling is anticipated on the given information; hold piling in reserve only if the
  boreholes reveal a soft layer thicker than ~2 m beneath the cafeteria or a high perched
  water table.

---

## 2. Footprint and zoning (finalised)

**Concept: a single compact 2-storey main block with a clearly separated, single-storey
cafeteria wing.**

- **Footprint:** main block roughly **45 m × 30 m (~1,350 m² per floor)** plus a
  cafeteria wing of roughly **25 m × 18 m (~450 m²)**, leaving generous circulation, a
  forecourt and service access within the 60 m × 60 m plot. Total built area in the order
  of **3,100–3,200 m²** — a reasonable mid-sized faculty. A single-storey scheme would
  consume most of the plot and leave no room for the service yard and drainage, so two
  storeys is the working assumption.

**Zoning logic (three bands):**
1. **Public/teaching band (front):** entrance foyer, lecture halls and classrooms at
   ground level, arranged off a central circulation spine. Lecture halls want clear spans,
   high ceilings and controlled daylight — they are the acoustic and structural priority.
2. **Staff/quiet band (rear or upper floor):** staff offices and meeting rooms, away from
   the noisiest teaching and from the cafeteria. Offices suit the upper floor, where they
   also benefit from daylight and views.
3. **Cafeteria band (separate wing, ground floor, service edge):** placed at the plot edge
   with its own external entrance and a dedicated **service yard / delivery route**, so
   that food deliveries, waste and grease collection never cross the teaching circulation.
   This separation is deliberate: it is the cheapest way to satisfy both hygiene and fire
   compartmentation requirements (§5).

**Placement of the cafeteria wing (finalised).** The cafeteria is the heaviest and most
service-dense block, so it is placed on the **most uniform part of the plot** as revealed
by the borehole grid, and its wing is kept structurally and fire-separated from the
teaching block. *(This siting rule is adopted from the Medicine survey — see §6.)*

**Circulation.** A single central spine with two stairs and a lift; the cafeteria wing
connects to the spine through a **fire-rated lobby** rather than opening directly onto
teaching circulation.

**External works.** Forecourt and drop-off at the front; service yard and bin store at
the rear of the cafeteria wing; a shaded outdoor seating terrace adjacent to the dining
area. All external circulation step-free (max 1:20 ramps where levels change).

**Structural grid.** A regular bay (indicatively 7.5–8.5 m) so that classrooms, offices
and the cafeteria dining hall all land on the same grid, with lecture halls spanning two
bays where a clear span is needed. Repetitive foundations are exactly what the layered-soil
condition rewards.

---

## 3. Primary construction materials — general building (finalised)

- **Structure:** reinforced-concrete frame (columns, beams, flat or beam-and-slab slabs)
  on shallow pad/strip footings. Rationale: it suits the flat stratified site and spread
  footings; it is robust and low-maintenance; it gives inherent fire resistance without
  added protection; it provides acoustic mass between stacked teaching floors; and a
  stiff, monolithic frame tolerates and redistributes the small differential movements
  that the layered soil makes a live risk. A steel frame with intumescent or board
  protection is a viable alternative for speed, but concrete is the better default here.
- **Floors:** suspended concrete slabs; screed and finish to suit use. No suspended timber
  floors in teaching or circulation areas.
- **External envelope:** a **drained and back-ventilated** rainscreen, or a rendered
  masonry/concrete-block cavity wall with insulation. On an exposed flat site the priority
  is a drained, back-ventilated construction with good weather detailing at openings,
  rather than a face-sealed system.
